title: 1816: The Year Without a Summer, with Dr. Helen Marsh
creator: Footnotes of History
description:
In 1815 Mount Tambora erupted, and a year later snow fell in June across New England and crops failed across Europe. Historian Dr. Helen Marsh explains what happened, who suffered, and how a cold, wet summer gave us Frankenstein.

Further reading: Helen's book, Ash and Frost (2024).

Support the show on Patreon: https://patreon.com/footnotesofhistory

sentences.t: Hello and welcome to Footnotes of History, I'm Sam Whitlock.
Today we're going back to 1816, which people at the time called the year without a summer, and some people called eighteen hundred and froze to death.
Which is a great nickname, honestly.
My guest is Dr. Helen Marsh, a historian of climate and food, and the author of Ash and Frost.
Helen, thanks for coming on.
Thanks for having me, Sam, this is my favourite year to talk about, which says a lot about me.
So, where does the story start?
It starts in April 1815, on an island in what's now Indonesia, with Mount Tambora.
And Tambora is not a small eruption, it's the largest eruption in recorded history.
People heard the explosions more than a thousand miles away and thought they were cannon fire.
Locally, it's devastating, tens of thousands of people die from the eruption itself and then the famine afterwards.
But the bit that reaches the rest of the world is the sulfur that goes up into the stratosphere.
Right, and that spreads around the whole globe.
It spreads into this thin veil that reflects sunlight back, and it takes about a year to really make itself felt.
So by the spring of 1816, average temperatures in parts of the northern hemisphere are down by maybe half a degree to a degree.
Which doesn't sound like much.
It doesn't sound like much, but it's enough to wreck a growing season, especially when it comes as these sudden cold snaps.

Okay, Helen, snow in June.
Snow in June, yes, so in early June 1816 there's a cold wave across New England and parts of Canada.
There are diaries from Vermont where farmers write about snow on the ground and ice on the ponds in the second week of June.
And their corn is already in the ground.
It's already in, it's already sprouted, and it just dies.
And then it happens again in July, and again in August, so even people who replant lose that crop too.
What does that do to people?
In New England it pushes a lot of families to give up and move west, into Ohio and beyond, so it actually shapes migration.
In Europe it's much worse, because Europe is already exhausted from the Napoleonic Wars.
Harvests fail, grain prices double or triple, and there are food riots in Britain, in France, in Switzerland.
And people at the time didn't know about Tambora, right, they had no idea why this was happening?
No idea at all, the connection between the eruption and the weather isn't really made until much later, the early twentieth century.
So at the time people blame all sorts of things, sunspots, divine punishment, even lightning rods.
Lightning rods?
Lightning rods, there were people who genuinely argued that Benjamin Franklin's invention had disturbed the natural electricity of the earth.
That's wonderful.
It's wonderful, and it tells you how frightening it was, people were reaching for any explanation they could find.
Switzerland was hit especially hard, wasn't it?
Switzerland is terrible, there are reports of people eating grass and moss, and the government ends up importing grain at enormous cost.
And this is also where the famous literary bit happens.
Yes, so on Lake Geneva that summer you have Mary Shelley, Percy Shelley, Lord Byron and his doctor, John Polidori, staying in a villa.
And it rains, and rains, and rains, so they're stuck indoors.
And Byron suggests they each write a ghost story.
And Mary Shelley comes up with Frankenstein.
She does, and Polidori writes The Vampyre, which is one of the first modern vampire stories.
So a volcano on the other side of the world gives us two of the great horror stories.
I love that, and I think it's a good reminder that these disasters don't stay in one place, they ripple.
Helen, this has been wonderful, thank you so much.
Thank you, Sam, it's been a pleasure.
